newsitem.title: USA: US court suspends long-distance phone rule.
newsitem.headline: US court suspends long-distance phone rule.

text.p: A federal appeals court here has temporarily suspended the Federal Communications Commission's decision to scrap a Depression-era rule that required long-distance phone companies to notify the agency beforehand of rate changes.

The court's action, disclosed by FCC officials Wednesday, came after the agency last October eliminated a 1934 rule that forced long-distance carriers to tell regulators ahead of time of plans to change rates or offer new services. The notifications to the FCC were made via "tariff" filings.

The FCC had argued its new approach was meant to inject more competition into the $80 billion long-distance market and cut thousands of pages of government red tape for long-distance carriers such as AT&T Corp and MCI Communications Corp.

But industry officials and consumer advocates had complained that the new rule -- scheduled to take effect in September -- would lead to consumer confusion and make it tougher for consumers to get the best possible deal.
The appeals court, without any comment, issued its "stay" last Thursday while it considers whether to overturn the rule. The court will hear arguments in the case.
MCI had requested the action and it hailed the suspension.
"MCI believes, as do many consumer groups, that tariffs protect consumers," said a company spokesperson.
"Consumers benefit from knowing what long-distance rates are industry-wide and whether companies are fulfilling their obligations under the law."
